questions.question: Buoys moored in the open sea record the sea's temperature as a slow hurricane crawls over them. By the time the storm has lingered for a day, the sea's surface beneath it has cooled by about 4 degrees Celsius. What cooled it?
questions.answer: Colder water churned up from below by its winds
choices: Colder water churned up from below by its winds
Ice falling into the sea from its frozen cloud tops
Cold air swept in from the poles by its winds
The low air pressure at the centre of the storm
questions.context: A hurricane's winds churn the top of the sea, mixing its warm surface layer with the colder water beneath it, so a slow storm can cool the sea under it by a few degrees and leave a trail of cooler water, a cold wake, behind it; that is why forecasters watch how deep the warm water goes, not only how warm the surface is. Ice from the frozen cloud tops melts long before it reaches the sea, a hurricane is a warm-cored storm of tropical seas that draws in no polar air, and its low pressure lifts the sea a little, about a centimetre for each hectopascal, rather than chilling it.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (TEKS 8.10C, the oceans' role in hurricanes; curriculum line G8.E6) teaches the warm sea as a hurricane's fuel and its weakening over cooler water; the cold wake is the storm cooling that sea itself.

questions.question: Warm, moist air rises into a hurricane's towering clouds, and kilometres up, its water vapour condenses into cloud droplets. What does the condensing do to the air around it?
questions.answer: Warms it, setting free heat the vapour held
choices: Warms it, setting free heat the vapour held
Cools it, as making droplets takes in heat
Cools it, as the droplets shade it from the Sun
Leaves it no warmer and no cooler
questions.context: Sea water takes in heat as it evaporates, and the vapour carries that heat up hidden inside it; when the vapour condenses into droplets the heat is set free, about 2.5 million joules for every kilogram of water, warming the air so that it rises faster and draws in more moist air from the sea. That is why meteorologists call a hurricane a heat engine, turning the sea's heat into the motion of its winds. Making droplets gives heat out; it is evaporation that takes heat in.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (TEKS 8.10C) teaches how the ocean powers a hurricane: vapour from the warm sea condenses in rising air and releases the heat that drives the storm.

questions.question: The sea along the equator is often warm enough to feed a hurricane. Yet hurricanes almost never form within about 5 degrees of latitude of the equator. What stops them there?
questions.answer: Earth's spin barely twists the air there
choices: Earth's spin barely twists the air there
The air there sinks instead of rising
The air there is too dry to build clouds
The winds there blow too hard for storms
questions.context: A hurricane needs a twist to set it turning, and Earth's spin gives moving air that twist (the Coriolis effect), which is zero at the equator and grows toward the poles. The equator's air is in fact humid and rising, full of thunderstorms, and its winds are often light, the calm belt sailors called the doldrums. Only a very few storms, such as Typhoon Vamei in 2001, have ever formed closer in.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade teaches that Earth's spin sets a hurricane turning, which is why they form over warm water but away from the equator (curriculum line G8.E6).

questions.question: Weather satellites watching from above see the hurricanes north of the equator turning counter-clockwise. Satellites watch the tropical cyclones south of the equator too. Which way do those storms turn?
questions.answer: Clockwise, the mirror of the storms in the north
choices: Clockwise, the mirror of the storms in the north
Counter-clockwise, the same as the storms in the north
Counter-clockwise, but more slowly than in the north
Either way, with each one's turn set by chance
questions.context: Earth's spin turns moving air one way north of the equator and the other way south of it, so the air rushing in toward a storm's centre swirls counter-clockwise in the north and clockwise in the south, every time. A draining sink is another matter: it is far too small for Earth's spin to steer, so its swirl can go either way.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade teaches that Earth's rotation sets a hurricane's spin, counter-clockwise north of the equator and clockwise south of it (curriculum line G8.E6).

questions.question: Hurricane John formed in the Pacific off Mexico in August 1994 and lasted about a month. Partway through its life, forecasters began calling it Typhoon John. What did the new name mark?
questions.answer: It had moved into another part of the ocean
choices: It had moved into another part of the ocean
Its winds had grown faster than a hurricane's
It had grown larger than a hurricane can be
It had begun to spin the other way round
questions.context: Hurricane and typhoon are two regional names for one kind of storm, the tropical cyclone: it is a hurricane in the Atlantic and the eastern and central Pacific, and a typhoon in the western Pacific. John was renamed when it crossed the International Date Line, where the western Pacific begins, and when it drifted back east in September it was Hurricane John again. Its winds, size and spin had nothing to do with the name.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (TEKS 8.10C, current wording) teaches tropical cyclones as hurricanes and typhoons: the same storm, named by the ocean it is in (curriculum line G8.E6).

questions.question: Joseph Duckworth, an Army pilot, flew a small two-seat trainer into a hurricane on the Texas coast in 1943, the first known flight made on purpose into a hurricane. After violent bumps and pounding rain, the plane broke out into the storm's eye, calm air with the Sun above and the ground in view below. Why is the sky in the eye clear?
questions.answer: Its air sinks, and sinking air makes no clouds
choices: Its air sinks, and sinking air makes no clouds
Its air rises too fast for clouds to form
Its low pressure keeps clouds from forming
Cold air pools there and holds off the clouds
questions.context: In the eye, air from high in the storm sinks slowly, warming and drying as it falls, so no clouds can form, and the winds die to light breezes. The eye has the lowest pressure in the storm, yet low pressure alone cannot clear the sky: all around the eye, in the ring of towering thunderstorms called the eyewall, air rises and builds cloud. The eye is the storm's warm core, several degrees warmer than the air around it, and on a second flight that day the weather officer William Jones-Burdick recorded temperatures inside the storm.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade teaches the hurricane's calm eye inside the eyewall (curriculum line G8.E6), and how we know it, from aircraft flown into the storm.

questions.question: A weather station on a low island lies straight in a hurricane's path. For hours its instruments record a roaring wind from the north-east. Then, within minutes, the wind drops almost to calm and blue sky shows overhead. What will the instruments most likely record next?
questions.answer: Fierce winds again, from the opposite way
choices: Fierce winds again, from the opposite way
Fierce winds again, from the same way
Light winds, as the storm has blown out
Light rain, as the outer rain bands pass
questions.context: The calm is the eye, and all around it lies the eyewall, a ring of towering thunderstorms with the storm's strongest winds. The winds circle the centre, so once the eye has passed, the far side of the eyewall strikes the station from the opposite direction, as fierce as before. Sailors of old took the eye's calm for the end of the storm, and forecasters still warn that the worst winds return soon after the eye passes.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade teaches the hurricane's eye and eyewall (curriculum line G8.E6): a calm centre ringed by the strongest winds.

questions.question: Herbert Saffir, an engineer, and Robert Simpson, a meteorologist, made a scale in the early 1970s that sorts hurricanes into five categories. In its form since 2010, the scale leaves out the danger that is often the deadliest, so a storm's category can badly understate how deadly it will be. Which danger is that?
choices: Its storm surge
Its strongest winds
Its tornadoes
Its flying debris
questions.context: Since 2010 the Saffir-Simpson scale has rated a storm by its strongest steady winds alone, so it says nothing of the storm surge, the rise of the sea that the winds push ashore; surge caused about half the deaths in US Atlantic hurricanes and tropical storms from 1963 to 2012, against 8 percent for wind and 3 for tornadoes. The scale's own descriptions do warn of the flying debris its winds hurl. Hurricane Ike was only a Category 2 as it neared Texas in 2008, yet it drove in a surge typical of a Category 4 or 5.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (curriculum line G8.E6; NGSS MS-ESS3-2 on natural hazards) teaches storm surge as a hurricane's great danger, and the Saffir-Simpson categories.

questions.question: Dropsondes, instrument packs that hurricane hunters drop by parachute to radio back the wind, show a hurricane's winds weakening day by day as it drifts north over sea water of 20 degrees Celsius. Another hurricane weakens too after it moves ashore. What do the two have in common?
questions.answer: Each has lost its supply of warm, moist air
choices: Each has lost its supply of warm, moist air
Each has moved where Earth's spin is weaker
Each has met cold air that freezes its clouds
Each gets too little sunlight to keep going
questions.context: A hurricane runs on warm, moist air off a warm sea, and neither cool water nor land can supply it, so the storm runs down; over land, the rough ground slows its winds as well. Earth's spin grows stronger, not weaker, away from the equator, and a hurricane's high cloud tops are frozen already, at about -70 degrees Celsius. Its fuel is the warm sea's moist air, not the sunlight falling on its clouds.
questions.grade_note: 8th grade (TEKS 8.10C) teaches that the warm ocean powers a hurricane, so it weakens once it moves over land or cold water.

e74ea6197e.why: Judge (medium, tell): the stem put the heat 'inside the storm's towering clouds', so a student who knew only the T1 water-cycle fact (clouds form by condensation) could pick 'Water vapour condensing into droplets' without knowing that condensation gives out heat, and the key was the-water-cycle's keyed answer. As the judge proposed, the stem now gives the condensing and asks what it does to the air, with warming and cooling choices so that the mechanism decides (F6-F8). Two changes from the judge's fix: 'heat engine' moves from the stem to the context, since it points at heat being given out; the key reads 'setting free heat the vapour held' rather than 'with heat the vapour carried up from the sea', so that it does not echo the stem's sea; and 'Warms it, by friction as the droplets fall' becomes 'Leaves it no warmer and no cooler', since falling drops really do warm the air a little by friction, which would make it partly true.

f864aa8288.why: Judge (high): the 'and why' half re-keyed the winds unit's Coriolis direction (1db7e2b5cb), and the stem asked two things. The question now asks the turn alone, with the judge's choices; the context still gives the reason, but without the right-and-left direction that 1db7e2b5cb keys. 'Every hurricane' became 'the hurricanes', so that the northern storms' sameness does not rule out the chance choice.

827ed3db90.why: Judge (medium, clarity): the stem asked why the eye is calm and clear, but the key explains only the clear sky, so 'Winds from every side meet there and cancel' looked fair for the calm. The question now asks one thing, 'Why is the sky in the eye clear?', with the judge's choices: the cancelling-winds choice becomes 'Its low pressure keeps clouds from forming', live because the eye's pressure is the lowest, and the context answers it (F31). Fact-check (uncertain): the stem now says 'the first known flight made on purpose into a hurricane', since reaching the eye may have been an accident, and the context says Jones-Burdick 'recorded temperatures inside the storm' (F27). The stem names the eye as the plane breaks out into it. Key unchanged.

0d9861f5f8.why: Judge (medium, tell): 'Its lightning' was a weak choice, leaving only surge and tornadoes live. Replaced, as the judge proposed, by 'Its flying debris', a wind-borne danger students fear that the wind scale does cover: its own category descriptions warn of flying debris (F30), as the context now says. 'Its strongest winds' kept, not reworded to gusts. Stem and key unchanged.

280cc72789.why: Judge (low, clarity): the dropsonde clause did no work; it now carries the how-we-know (the dropsondes show the winds weakening), as the judge proposed. Fact-check (optional): 'weakens just as fast' ashore became 'weakens too', since decay over land is often faster. The context no longer says the vapour condenses and releases its heat, which would give away 98bfb751c5's key. Key and choices unchanged.

added.5a52a8a4e8: Replaces 4ed68556f0, on the judge's alternative: a slow storm cools the sea beneath it by churning up colder water from below (the cold wake), a T4 mechanism of the warm sea as fuel that no unit keys (F28, with F1, F10, F23, F29, F32). The judge's first choice, the spiral rain bands, was not used: every draft of it let the stem rule out the eye and the eyewall (the town far from the eye, the bursts of rain), and the history of their first sighting by radar could not be sourced. Wrong choices: ice from the frozen cloud tops (it melts long before the sea, F32), polar air (a hurricane is warm-cored and non-frontal, F29), low pressure (it lifts the sea, F23). Sinking air in the eye was not used as a choice, since it would hint 827ed3db90's key. The context does not say why the cooling weakens the storm, so it does not give away c5a0ce3a94.

dropped.question: North of the equator the longest day of the year comes in June, yet the Atlantic's hurricanes are most common in early September, nearly three months later. Why do they come so late?
dropped.why: Judge (high): it re-asked the T2 why-we-have-seasons question on the sea's slow seasonal warming, with the same key ('The oceans are slow to warm up') and two of its wrong choices (Earth nearest the Sun, the Sun hottest then). The fact is T2's at the same depth, so it cannot be re-keyed here without re-asking it; replaced by an added question on the cold wake (F28).
